sections.title: GInI Implementation: Reach, Intensity, and Fidelity
sections.intro: Plain-language guide: This section asks how widely the GInI-aligned approach has been implemented (reach), how much implementation support was provided (intensity), and how closely implementation followed the intended approach (fidelity). Adaptations are intentional changes made to fit local needs or conditions.

sections.title: Linked Initiative Contribution Record
sections.intro: Evidence instruction: Complete this record using the strongest evidence reasonably available. Formal evaluation or quantitative impact analysis is not required unless it exists. Where evidence is unavailable, record this explicitly rather than estimating or reconstructing unsupported values. Add one record per selected initiative; include successful, mixed, and stopped initiatives.

sections.title: GInI-Aligned Outcomes and Evidence Register
sections.intro: Measurement rule. Use the strongest available organizational evidence. Quantitative records are preferred where they exist, but their absence does not prevent completion. Do not estimate or reconstruct unavailable data solely for this survey. Where quantitative measurement is unavailable, identify the best available qualitative or documentary evidence and classify its evidence level. Missing baseline, follow-up, comparison, or verification data must be recorded as “Not Available”. A change is not automatically caused by GInI implementation. External-impact rule: at organization/ program level, record at least one material external outcome where the assessed innovation program is intended to create external value; otherwise document why external impact is not applicable to the assessed scope.

groups.title: G.1 Innovation Program Outcome Families
groups.note: No automatic weighting or aggregation applies to indicators within an Outcome Family. Report each material indicator separately, with its own definition/ unit, baseline (if available), current value or qualitative evidence, source, and E0–E5 evidence level. Do not average indicators with different units. If only qualitative evidence exists, record it without inventing numbers. Evidence levels describe the support for a claim, not the magnitude of performance.

groups.title: G.2 Outcome Evidence Register
groups.note: Record the strongest available evidence for each material outcome. Quantitative evidence is not mandatory where it does not exist. Classify every outcome. At least one external classification is required at organization/ program level where external value is within scope.

J13–J15 represent progressively advanced evaluation capability and are not expected to be available in every participating organization.

glossary.def: An intentional change to the planned implementation approach to make it more suitable for a particular unit, context, population, or emerging condition.
A negative or unexpected effect associated with an initiative, including effects on people, society, the environment, partners, or the organization.
A person, group, community, organization, or other party that experiences, or may experience, an effect from an organizational decision, activity, or innovation.
The extent to which an observed outcome can credibly be said to have been caused by a particular initiative or intervention, rather than by other factors.
Loss of participants, units, or data between evaluation waves, or failure to respond. Results can be distorted if those lost or not responding differ from those who remain.
Starting with a preferred future state and working backward to identify the milestones, capabilities, decisions, and actions needed to move toward it.
In the GInI-aligned outcome families, the mix of the innovation portfolio across units, innovation types, risk levels, and time horizons.
The starting value or condition measured before, or at the beginning of, an intervention so that later change can be assessed.
The process of checking whether the expected value or benefits of an innovation were actually achieved after implementation.

A statement that one factor caused or materially produced another. In this survey, the permitted claim level (descriptive, temporal association, comparative, contribution, causal-supportive, or causal) must be limited by the quality of the evidence and the evaluation design actually available.

GInI organizational certification schemes referenced in this survey: CInOrg is the private-sector-oriented scheme, and CGInO is the government-oriented scheme. Recording them here does not make this survey an official assessment.
Grouping in the data, such as several respondents from the same unit, whose answers are likely to be related. Analysis must account for this so that results are not overstated.
Another program, policy, investment, restructuring, technology change, or external action occurring during the same period that may also influence the observed outcome.
See Comparison Unit or Group.
A reasonably similar unit, organization, population, or group used to help judge what might have happened without the initiative or with different implementation exposure.
A factor other than the initiative being assessed that may influence both implementation and the outcome, making the relationship harder to interpret.
A situation in which units intended for comparison are partly exposed to the implementation, making differences between groups harder to interpret.
A supported judgment that an initiative played a meaningful role in producing an outcome, while recognizing that other factors may also have contributed.
In the GInI-aligned outcome families, the quantity, quality, and value of opportunities that advance through the innovation pipeline toward implementation.
Costs that the organization or its stakeholders would otherwise have incurred and that were prevented by an initiative.
The best available indication of what would likely have happened in the absence of the initiative or intervention being assessed.
A measured characteristic, such as unit size, sector, or region, that is taken into account in an analysis so that comparisons are fairer.
How benefits, costs, and harms are shared across different groups, including whether some groups gain while others bear burdens.
Response used when the respondent lacks sufficient knowledge to answer. It is never treated as a score of zero.
A change in the wider network of partners, suppliers, institutions, markets, communities, or other actors with which the organization interacts.
A numerical estimate of the size and direction of a change associated with an intervention, usually accompanied by information about uncertainty.
In the GInI-aligned outcome families, innovation outputs relative to the inputs, time, and cost required, including how promptly weak initiatives are stopped or redirected.
A precise statement of the effect an evaluation intends to estimate: for which outcome, population, intervention or exposure, comparison, time period, and effect measure.
A defined point or period when implementation or outcome data are collected, such as baseline, six-month follow-up, or annual review.
The strength of the information available to support a claim, ranging in this survey from no evidence (E0) to advanced impact evidence (E5).
An evaluation in which units are assigned at random to receive the implementation or not, allowing the strongest test of cause and effect.
See Implementation Exposure.

A meaningful positive or adverse change beyond the organization that is associated with an innovation initiative or program and matters to external stakeholders, society, the environment, markets, or public value.
A change experienced outside the organization by customers, citizens, beneficiaries, communities, partners, markets, ecosystems, the environment, public institutions, or society.
The extent to which the organization’s innovations continue to address real and changing needs, expectations, conditions, and challenges outside the organization.
The extent to which implementation was delivered and used as originally intended, while documenting any justified adaptations.
A later measurement taken after implementation to determine whether conditions or outcomes changed over time.
A structured approach that uses foresight, preferred futures, pathways, portfolios, partnerships, and adaptive governance to influence future conditions rather than only predict them.
Putting the intended innovation-management approach into actual organizational practice, rather than only planning or documenting it.
The GInI-aligned practices, training, tools, governance, and support that a person, team, unit, or organization actually received or experienced.
How much implementation activity or support was received, such as training hours, coaching, workshops, tools, leadership attention, or frequency of use.
How much of the intended population or organization was actually reached, for example the number or percentage of targeted people, roles, teams, or units participating.
The organization’s practical ability to identify opportunities, develop and test ideas, make evidence- informed decisions, implement innovations, learn, and create value repeatedly.
The collection of innovation initiatives managed together so that resources, risk, time horizons, strategic fit, and expected value can be balanced.
In the GInI-aligned outcome families, the quantity, quality, strategic value, and diversity of the opportunities and ideas entering the innovation pipeline, plus the participant time involved.
See Implementation Intensity.
A result experienced mainly inside the organization, such as improved efficiency, capability, engagement, governance, cost, or decision quality.
Data collected from the same or comparable units at more than one point in time, allowing change and trends to be examined.
Important enough to influence decisions because of the significance of an issue, impact, risk, opportunity, or stakeholder concern.
Confidence that a measure means the same thing across groups, languages, units, or periods, so that comparisons between them are fair.
The smallest change that an evaluation could reliably detect, given its sample size and data quality.
An evaluation approach that combines quantitative evidence, such as indicators, with qualitative evidence, such as interviews or case documentation.
Response used when an item genuinely does not apply to the assessed unit or to the respondent’s role.
Response used when the requested information or evidence does not exist in the organization. It is recorded as an evidence gap and must not be estimated or reconstructed.

A change that follows from an activity or innovation, such as improved service quality, behavior, capability, wellbeing, resilience, or environmental performance. An outcome is different from an output, which is the immediate deliverable produced.
The balance of an initiative’s intended or observed outcomes between internal organizational benefit and external stakeholder or societal value.
The immediate product, service, process, policy, prototype, capability, or other deliverable produced by an innovation activity.

ISO/ UNDP PAS 53002:2024, a publicly available specification giving guidance on how organizations contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. This survey is aligned with it for research use but does not assess conformity.
A check that applies the analysis where no effect should exist, such as a period before implementation. Finding an apparent effect there signals a problem with the method.
Whether an estimated change is large enough to matter in real terms to the organization or its stakeholders, regardless of statistical significance.
The direction in which an outcome was already moving before implementation began. It must be considered before later change is attributed to the initiative.
Recording an evaluation plan in a dated, unalterable form before results are known, so that any later changes are visible.
Value created for society or the public through better outcomes, access, trust, equity, resilience, policy effectiveness, or responsible use of public resources.
An evaluation that does not use random assignment but uses careful comparison, such as phased rollout or matched units, to approximate a test of cause and effect.
See Implementation Reach.
Repeating an analysis in different reasonable ways to see whether the conclusion still holds.
A coherent description of a plausible future used to explore uncertainty, test assumptions, and improve decisions; it is not a prediction.
One of the 17 United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, each with specific targets and indicators.
Distortion that arises when the units receiving implementation differ systematically from those that do not, for reasons that also affect outcomes.
An analytical check that tests whether conclusions remain similar when assumptions, model specifications, data rules, or comparison choices are changed.
An observable development or indicator monitored because it may show that an assumed future condition is emerging or changing.
A broader change affecting communities or society, including social, economic, environmental, institutional, cultural, or wellbeing effects.
A measure of how much an estimate would be expected to vary by chance. Smaller values indicate a more precise estimate.
The ability of a study or analysis to detect a meaningful effect when one truly exists, given the amount and quality of available data.
Structured scanning frameworks covering social, technological, economic, environmental, political, and legal factors; STEEPL also includes ethical factors.
Testing a strategy, initiative, or portfolio against different plausible future conditions to identify vulnerabilities, trade-offs, and adaptation needs.
Examining results separately for particular groups, such as units, regions, or stakeholder types, to see whether effects differ between them.
The extent to which an implemented practice continues to be used, supported, reviewed, and improved over time.
Systematic monitoring of emerging developments, practices, and technologies, inside and outside the organization’s sector.
Projecting how identified trends may develop and combine, in order to inform future options and decisions.
Checking a finding against several different sources or methods to see whether they point to the same conclusion.
A numerical range showing the uncertainty around an estimated effect. Wider intervals generally indicate greater uncertainty.
The full set of activities, suppliers, partners, and users involved in creating and delivering the organization’s products, services, or policies.
A review of evidence by someone sufficiently independent from the activity being assessed to check its accuracy, completeness, or credibility.
An early, incomplete, or emerging indication of a possible future change that may become strategically important.
